What it does

- HEVC → MP4 recording via your existing FFmpeg (not bundled). Files land in recordzy/recordings/ as recordzy-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.mp4.

- Pause-menu controls (Replay Mod style): Start/Stop + Pause/Resume buttons, plus F6 (start/stop) and F7 (pause/resume) keybinds, and a small REC HUD indicator.

- Mod Menu + Cloth Config screen — defaults 720p / 60fps / 8 Mbps, configurable up to 1080p, 30–90 fps, 1–50 Mbps, and encoder choice.

The optimization (your main ask)

1. GPU downscale before readback — the window framebuffer is blitted to a small target-resolution FBO (flipped in the same blit), so only the reduced pixels ever hit the CPU.

2. Async PBO ping-pong — two Pixel Buffer Objects hide GPU→CPU latency; glReadPixels never stalls the render thread.

3. Off-thread encoding — frames go through a bounded queue to a dedicated FFmpeg writer thread.

4. FPS-gated capture + frame dropping if the encoder falls behind, and a reusable buffer pool (no per-frame GC stutter).

For your phone (Snapdragon 7s Gen 2 / ZalithLauncher) In the config, set the encoder to hevc_mediacodec to use the hardware HEVC encoder for near-zero CPU cost. The default libx265 / ultrafast works as a fallback.

## Turn 14 — Jun 24, 9:13 AM ·Jun 24

**🧑 User:**

Would it lag if I use mediacodec if it even works?

**🤖 Kiro:**

Hardware encoding via MediaCodec should eliminate the lag since the dedicated video encoder on the device handles the work instead of taxing the CPU, so the encoding bottleneck that was causing your previous performance issues should largely disappear.

That said, there are still some costs that remain independent of the encoder itself: the framebuffer readback that happens every frame still requires GPU/CPU work, the color space conversion from RGB to YUV happens on the CPU per-frame, and there's some GPU bandwidth contention between the game and the hardware encoder. These aren't zero-cost, but they're much smaller than software encoding overhead. So you should see a dramatic improvement—likely jumping from your degraded 42fps up to a stable, near-native framerate—though it won't be completely lag-free. Plus, the VFR fix means even if it can't sustain 60fps, it'll stay smooth and consistent rather than spiraling downward.Short version: it should be dramatically smoother than libx265/libx264 — most of your lag goes away — but it won't be literally zero overhead. Here's the honest breakdown.

Why it'll lag far less Your lag so far has been dominated by software encoding (libx265 chewing CPU cores that the game needs). hevc_mediacodec hands encoding to the dedicated hardware video-encoder block on the Snapdragon 7s Gen 2 — a separate silicon unit that isn't your CPU or your render thread. A chip like that encodes 1080p60 HEVC basically for free. So the single biggest cost in your current setup essentially disappears, and the "42fps + degrading" problem should be gone (the death-spiral bug is already fixed separately by the VFR change).

What still costs something (encoder-independent) These happen no matter which encoder you pick:

1. Framebuffer readback — every captured frame, RecordZy reads Minecraft's framebuffer (via the screenshot path) and copies it to the CPU. This is the main remaining cost and is unrelated to the encoder.

2. Color conversion — FFmpeg converts your rgb24 frames to nv12/yuv420p for MediaCodec (a per-frame CPU pass; modest at 720p, more at 1080p).

3. GPU/memory bandwidth sharing — the HW encoder and the game share memory bandwidth, but the impact is small compared to CPU software encoding.

4. MobileGlues translation overhead on the readback.

Realistic expectation

- 720p: should feel close to your normal (non-recording) framerate.

- 1080p: more readback + conversion cost, but the encoder still won't be the bottleneck — so likely still much better than libx265 ever was. With hardware encoding you could realistically try 1080p/60 and have it be usable, which was hopeless on software HEVC.

Two caveats (already flagged)

- It has to work first — the Adreno color-format quirk might require feeding nv12; if it errors on-device, I'll add an nv12 path to RecordZy's ffmpeg command.

- If, after HW encoding, the readback becomes the remaining bottleneck, I can optimize the capture next (reduce the per-frame copy / downscale cost) — that's the logical next step once we confirm mediacodec runs.

So: try it once the APK builds. If it's smooth — great, the encoder was the problem. If there's still noticeable lag, it's now the capture path, and that's a separate, fixable target.

CURRENT REFACTOR (the optimization request) — JUST STARTED, CUT OFF MID-WAY:

- Goal: make the tee ON-DEMAND instead of always-on. Currently the tee is always active at launch (RecorderPrefs.isEnabled() defaults true), adding constant GPU overhead + latency even when NOT recording. The user's phone built-in recorder is smoother because it has zero impact when idle.

- New design: native renders DIRECTLY to display at launch (zero overhead). On Start: RenderThread creates EGL + capture SurfaceTexture (using a 1×1 pbuffer to get a current context first), calls JREUtils.setupBridgeWindow(captureSurface) to redirect native to capture, then creates the display WindowSurface (now free), then encoder, then composites. On Stop: stop encoder, release display WindowSurface, JREUtils.setupBridgeWindow(displaySurface) to redirect back, teardown.

- Safe failure mode: if setupBridgeWindow redirect doesn't take effect, eglCreateWindowSurface on the display will fail (two producers) → catch exception → abort recording, revert setupBridgeWindow(display). Normal play is NEVER harmed (native always renders direct to display when not recording).

- Feasibility rationale: MinecraftGLSurface.surfaceDestroyed is empty {} and re-attach just calls setupBridgeWindow(newSurface), so the native bridge handles window changes via setupBridgeWindow (renderer recreates its EGLSurface). So mid-game swap should work.

Looking at what causes lag during recording in always-on: every frame gets an extra fullscreen blit from the capture texture to display, plus the SurfaceTexture round trip, which adds latency even when not recording. The fundamental constraint is that we need separate draws to different EGL surfaces, so we can't avoid the double blit entirely.

The fragility comes from the fact that an OpenAL tap is not using a public, stable API — it's reaching into the guts of a native library that the launcher owns. Concretely:

1. The launcher ships its own libopenal.so, and we'd be replacing/patching it. ZalithLauncher bundles a specific build of OpenAL-soft. 2. We'd hook an internal function, not a documented one. The clean place to grab the final mixed PCM is OpenAL-soft's internal mix/output routine. A hook written against version X can fail to apply, grab the wrong buffer, or crash against version Y.

3. ABI / symbol coupling with the JNI bridge. Our JNI ring-buffer bridge depends on symbol names and the calling convention staying put. A different OpenAL-soft version, NDK, or compiler flags (inlining, etc.) can shift those out from under us.

On the MC side it's actually less fragile — because we tap the final mixed output, it doesn't matter what sounds MC plays or how. The risk is mostly the launcher/OpenAL layer, not the Minecraft version itself. A new LWJGL/OpenAL config in a future MC could in theory matter, but that's secondary.

Here's where things landed.

Done: game audio via route (b) — PR #18 ✓ (CI green) I built the OpenAL mixer tap exactly as we discussed. The launcher's libopenal.so turned out to be ideal for this — it's un-stripped and uses the OpenSL ES backend, so I could:

- Inline-hook ALCdevice::renderSamples with ShadowHook (the ByteDance sibling of the ByteHook your project already uses). It's a private symbol, but since the lib isn't stripped I resolve it from .symtab via shadowhook_dlsym_symtab().

- After the original renders each frame, copy the final mixed 16-bit PCM into a lock-free ring buffer → Java pump thread → hardware AAC encoder → 2nd track in the MP4, with video PTS anchored to a common start so audio/video stay in sync.

This captures exactly what Minecraft plays — game sounds and simple-voicechat playback — because it's the final mix. No permission prompt, no MediaProjection, no OpenAL rebuild.

Fail-safe: if the lib/symbol/hook isn't available, it returns false and recording silently falls back to video-only. The hook path can't break gameplay.

What you need to do This is the big native change I couldn't test locally (no NDK in my sandbox — CI only verifies it compiles). On your device, please check:

1. Recording now has audio that's in sync.

2. No new lag from the tap.

3. The earlier microstutter — first try setting record FPS to 30 (clean divisor of your 60), which should smooth the cadence regardless of this PR.

If audio is silent or desynced, grab a logcat filtered on RecordZyTap and GameRecorder and send it — the tags log whether the hook installed and at what sample rate, which tells me exactly where to look.

One open option if you want it later: a menu toggle to turn audio off (right now it defaults on), and an audio-PTS offset tweak if there's a constant lead/lag. Say the word.

Quick question, why do I have to manually like calibrate it?

**🤖 Kiro:**

The user is asking a fair question about why manual calibration is necessary instead of being automatic. I should explain honestly what makes it difficult to determine automatically — the audio lead is essentially the OpenAL/Android output latency, which represents how far ahead audio gets rendered and buffered before it's actually heard. I should also clarify whether I can make this automatic and offer to do so if possible.

The key insight is that we could query the actual device latency directly. OpenAL-soft exposes latency information through its APIs, and Android's AudioTrack has timestamp and latency methods available. Our OpenAL implementation already computes the buffered latency in the output layer — we could expose that value and use it automatically as the audio delay, making the calibration device-correct without manual intervention. While there's some nuance around mixer lag and video pipeline latency, the dominant factor is the OpenAL output buffer latency, so exposing that would give a solid automatic estimate.Honest answer: you have to calibrate it because the offset depends on your device, and the current build just guesses a fixed default (90 ms) instead of measuring it.

Here's the "why" in one paragraph: the audio is generated/buffered ahead of when your speaker actually plays it. The recorder timestamps each audio chunk at the moment it's captured (i.e., when OpenAL renders it), and each video frame at the moment it's displayed — so the audio lands ahead by however much audio output latency your device has. That latency isn't a fixed number: it changes with the device, the Android audio path (low-latency "fast" path vs. deep-buffer), the buffer sizes, the OS version, and especially the output route — Bluetooth/wireless earbuds add 100–300 ms, wired/speaker much less. There's no single value that's right everywhere, which is why I exposed a slider rather than baking in one number.

But your instinct is right — it shouldn't need manual tuning in the common case. I can make it auto-calibrate:

- The audio system actually knows its output latency. Our custom OpenAL build already computes it (OpenSLPlayback::getClockLatency() → buffered frames ÷ sample rate), and Android's AudioTrack/AAudio expose it too. I can have the tap report that live latency and use it as the automatic audio delay, so it's correct on your device with no slider fiddling.

- I'd keep the slider as a manual override / trim (and bonus: it'd still let you compensate for Bluetooth lag, which the system often under-reports).

So the plan would be: default = "Auto" (use the measured latency); slider = optional fine-tune.

Want me to implement the auto-calibration? It's a small addition to the OpenAL tap (expose the latency) plus the app using it — one more OpenAL rebuild + APK cycle. If you tell me the slider value that lined things up perfectly for you, I can also just make that the default and skip the rebuild. Your call.

Here's the situation, then 5 optimization methods ranked by impact so you can pick.

Why it's happening (the bottleneck) When recording, the launcher stops letting Minecraft draw straight to your screen. Instead, one GL thread now has to, for every game frame:

1. Copy the frame to screen (full-res textured pass + a vsync-locked swapBuffers), then

2. On paced frames, switch GL context again, draw a scaled copy into the HEVC encoder, and swapBuffers into it (which stalls if the chip's encoder is even slightly behind).

That's up to 2 context switches + 2 buffer swaps per frame on a single thread. When that thread can't finish 60×/sec, your displayed frames sag to ~24– 30 even though the game engine is making 41–60 — and the extra GPU pass steals time from the game itself, dropping in-game fps too.

The 5 methods (pick 1–2) Method 1 — Move encoding to its own GL thread (biggest win, most effort) The display thread does only copy-to-screen → swap. A second thread (shared GL context) samples the latest frame at your target fps and feeds the encoder independently. The encoder's context switch + the HEVC back- pressure stall can never touch the display path again.

- Fixes: both symptoms (choppy screen and in-game lag). Effort: medium-high. Risk: medium (cross-thread GL sync).

Method 2 — Give the GPU back to the game (low-priority recorder context) (tiny, high value) Create the recorder's EGL context at LOW priority (EGL_IMG_context_priority). Minecraft's renderer keeps GPU priority, so its fps recovers; the recorder just uses leftover GPU.

- Fixes: in-game fps mainly. Effort: ~10 lines. Risk: low (recording may get marginally choppier under heavy load).

Method 3 — Stop waiting for vsync on the screen copy (eglSwapInterval(0)) (tiny) Right now every screen swap blocks until the compositor's vsync. Setting swap interval to 0 lets the thread push frames as fast as the game makes them.

- Fixes: the "looks like 30fps" symptom if vsync-blocking is the limiter. Effort: ~3 lines. Risk: low-medium (possible minor tearing; some drivers ignore it).

Method 4 — Lighten the encoder (your SD 7s Gen 2 HEVC may be the staller) (low effort) Try H.264/AVC (often a faster hardware path than HEVC on mid Snapdragons), switch to CBR, and stretch the keyframe interval (2s → 4–5s). If encoder back-pressure is what's stalling the GL thread, this removes it.

- Fixes: in-game stutter from encoder stalls. Effort: low. Risk: low (slightly bigger files / less compression).

Method 5 — Trim per-frame loop overhead (cheap polish) Coalesce frame callbacks so the loop never runs more than once per produced frame, skip the redundant transform-matrix re-read, and drop the encoder pass off the display thread entirely (folds into #1).

- Fixes: modest gains. Effort: low. Risk: low.

My recommendation

- Want the real fix: pick Method 1 (optionally + Method 2). This is what makes it genuinely smooth.

- Want maximum gain for minimum risk/effort: pick Method 2 + Method 3 — both are tiny, ship fast, and hit both symptoms. Add Method 4 (try AVC) if your chip's HEVC encoder turns out to be the staller.

Done. Here's the summary.

Method 1 implemented: dedicated encoder thread ✓ I rebuilt the recording pipeline so the encoder can never stall your display again.

Before (the problem): one GL thread did everything per frame — present to screen and swap into the HEVC encoder. That encoder swap blocks whenever the chip's encoder falls behind, so your displayed frames dropped to ~24–30 and the extra work stole GPU time from Minecraft.

Now:

- Display thread → only presents your frame to the screen, then does a cheap offscreen render (FBO) of the frame into a shared texture. No encoder swap, so it physically cannot block on the encoder anymore.

- Encoder thread (brand new, shares the GL context) → grabs the newest shared frame and does the blocking encoder swap entirely on its own. If the encoder lags, it just drops a frame instead of freezing your view.

Safety details:

- Triple-buffered handoff so the encoder never reads a frame the display is mid-writing (frames drop cleanly under load instead of tearing/stalling).

- GPU fences (glFenceSync/glWaitSync) keep the two threads' GPU work correctly ordered without a CPU stall — this needed an ES3 context, so I upgraded EglCore.

- The relay pass is mathematically identical to the old single pass, so video orientation/scale are unchanged.

Status: Android CI (full matrix, all ABIs) and the Debug build are green — it compiles and builds. PR: https://github.com/Zack694/ZalithLauncher- Reborn/pull/37

What to test on device Record at 60fps and watch for:

1. Live view smoothness — the screen should now track much closer to your real in-game fps instead of looking like 30.

2. In-game fps — should recover since the recorder steals less GPU time.

Be honest with me on the result — I built and CI-verified it, but only you can confirm the on-device feel. If it's better but you want even more, we still have Method 2 (give the GPU priority back to the game) and Method 4 (try the H.264 encoder path) in reserve, and they stack cleanly on top of this.
